Author(s)</copyright-statement><copyright-year>2021</copyright-year><license><ali:license_ref xmlns:ali="http://www.niso.org/schemas/ali/1.0/" specific-use="textmining" content-type="ccbyncndlicense">https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/</ali:license_ref><license-p>This is an open access article under the CC BY-NC-ND license (http://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/).</license-p></license></permissions><self-uri xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" content-type="pmc-pdf" xlink:href="main.pdf"/><abstract id="abs0010"><p>The use of probiotics in gastrointestinal ailments has shown therapeutic effects. The imbalance of the microbiota caused by antibiotic treatment or others has been shown to be restored to normal with probiotic treatment. In this study, a genomically and phenotypically safe probiotic <italic toggle="yes">Alkalihalobacillus clausii</italic> 088AE has been evaluated for ameliorating antibiotic-associated diarrhea (AAD) in pediatrics (PE, n = 60, 2–10 years), adolescent and adults (AA, n = 60, 11–65 years) through a randomized controlled clinical trial. <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE was administered for seven days (PE, 4 and AA, 6 billion/day) and primary and secondary endpoints were evaluated on different visits. Compared to the respective placebo arms, <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE improved the diarrheal (<italic toggle="yes">t</italic>ime <italic toggle="yes">t</italic>o <italic toggle="yes">l</italic>ast <italic toggle="yes">u</italic>nformed <italic toggle="yes">s</italic>tool and diarrheal frequency) conditions in children, adolescents and adults. <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE treatment decreased AAD-severity score on visit 5 in both pediatric (0.12 ± 0.33, 12.39 folds), adult and adolescent (0.54 ± 0.36, 2.34 folds) groups compared to those respective placebo arm (p &lt; 0.05). <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE was well tolerated, did not cause significant changes in vital and clinical safety parameters and subjects reported no adverse effects or serious adverse reactions. <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE is safe and therapeutically effective against AAD, reducing onset of diarrhea and related severity symptoms including abdominal discomfort and pain, bloating and flatulence. <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE may be recommended as a live bio-therapeutic agent for improving clinical pathophysiology of gastrointestinal ailments, in particular antibiotic-associated diarrhea and related symptoms.</p></abstract><abstract abstract-type="teaser" id="abs0015"><p><italic toggle="yes">Alkalihalobacillus clausii</italic>, antibiotic-associated diarrhea, <italic toggle="yes">t</italic>ime <italic toggle="yes">t</italic>o <italic toggle="yes">l</italic>ast <italic toggle="yes">i</italic>nformed <italic toggle="yes">s</italic>tool, Bristol stool scale, adverse effects, efficacy.</p></abstract><kwd-group id="kwrds0010"><title>Keywords</title><kwd><italic toggle="yes">Alkalihalobacillus clausii</italic></kwd><kwd>Antibiotic-associated diarrhea</kwd><kwd>Time to last informed stool</kwd><kwd>Bristol stool scale</kwd><kwd>Adverse effects</kwd><kwd>Efficacy</kwd></kwd-group><custom-meta-group><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-status-qastatus</meta-name><meta-value>0</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-status-live</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-status-embargo</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-status-released</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-open-access</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-olf</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-manuscript</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-legally-suppressed</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-has-pdf</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-has-supplement</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-pdf-only</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-suppress-copyright</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-is-real-version</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-is-scanned-article</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-preprint</meta-name><meta-value>no</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-prop-in-epmc</meta-name><meta-value>yes</meta-value></custom-meta><custom-meta><meta-name>pmc-license-ref</meta-name><meta-value>CC BY-NC-ND</meta-value></custom-meta></custom-meta-group></article-meta></front><body><sec id="sec1"><label>1</label><title>Introduction</title><p id="p0010">Treatment with common and new antibiotics is becoming progressively ineffective and complicated due to rapid emergence of antimicrobial resistance. Antibiotic therapy has most prevalent adverse reactions such as antibiotic-associated diarrhea and other gastrointestinal, physiological and psychological illnesses [<xref rid="bib1" ref-type="bibr">1</xref>, <xref rid="bib2" ref-type="bibr">2</xref>]. Commonly associated symptoms of antibiotic-associated diarrhea are dehydration, fever, nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, watery diarrhea, bloody and foul-smelling diarrhea range from mild and self-limiting to severe. Clinically significant antibiotic-associated diarrhea may appear mushy (loose) or watery stools at least three episodes a day right after few hours up to two months of antibiotics intake [<xref rid="bib3" ref-type="bibr">3</xref>].</p><p id="p0015">The use of antibiotics systematically inducts a multimodal disturbances of the microbial ecology through the longitudinal decrease in the distribution, diversity and richness of autochthonous microorganisms in the gastrointestinal tract [<xref rid="bib4" ref-type="bibr">4</xref>, <xref rid="bib5" ref-type="bibr">5</xref>]. The aminoglycoside streptomycin can perturb the balance of microbiota and increases the abundance of phyla <italic toggle="yes">Bacteroidetes</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">Firmicutes</italic> [<xref rid="bib6" ref-type="bibr">6</xref>]. Ampicillin and ciprofloxacin augmented genus <italic toggle="yes">Acinetobacter</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus,</italic> respectively [<xref rid="bib7" ref-type="bibr">7</xref>]. Certain antibiotics can cause the proliferation of <italic toggle="yes">Fusobacteria</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">Clostridia</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">Eubacteria</italic> while demolishing beneficial groups like <italic toggle="yes">Bacteroides</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">Bifidobacteria</italic> [<xref rid="bib8" ref-type="bibr">8</xref>]. Such imbalance (<italic toggle="yes">dysbiosis</italic>) affects the microbial synergisms by depriving microbial network, nutrients, metabolites of microbial and host origin, promotes the horizontal transfer of antibiotic resistant genes (ARGs) and mobile genetic elements (MGEs) to sensitive microorganisms. The collapsed resident microbiota often fails to resist the overgrowth of endogenous opportunistic microorganisms and inhibit the pathogenic invasion. Re-establishment of normal gut microbiota happens over time after cessation of antibiotic therapy [<xref rid="bib9" ref-type="bibr">9</xref>]. The microbiota recovered after antibiotic treatment can be unstable and therefore patients can be susceptible to secondary infections and other diseases. Therefore, antibiotic-associated diarrhea can lead to prolonged hospitalization with persistent illness and increased cost of medical care [<xref rid="bib10" ref-type="bibr">10</xref>].</p><p id="p0020">Therefore, the restoration of normal gut microbiota is a fundamental therapeutic treatment paradigm, in which probiotics can provide promising healthcare solutions for antibiotic-associated diarrhea [<xref rid="bib11" ref-type="bibr">11</xref>]. Probiotics are potential live bio-therapeutics, which maintain intestinal microecology during or after antibiotic treatment through competition for epithelial receptors and nutrients, inhibition of epithelial and mucosal adhesion of pathogens, producing short chain fatty acids (SCFAs), balancing non-favorable intestinal pH (low), regulating immunity and synthesizing antimicrobial peptides and metabolites. With these mechanisms, probiotics provide a promising route to treat many gastrointestinal ailments including antibiotic-associated diarrhea without a risk of spreading antibiotic resistance among other microorganisms [<xref rid="bib12" ref-type="bibr">12</xref>, <xref rid="bib13" ref-type="bibr">13</xref>].</p><p id="p0025">The therapeutic effects of probiotics in the treatment of infectious and antibiotic-associated diarrhea have been evaluated through randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and meta-analysis [<xref rid="bib14" ref-type="bibr">14</xref>]. The probiotics intervention adopts either a monoculture or mixed culture formula and consists of a variety of microbial species, including <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus rhamnosus, Lactobacillus casei, Lactobacillus plantarum, Lactobacillus acidophilus, Bacillus coagulans, Bacillus clausii</italic> (current nomenclature <italic toggle="yes">Alkalihalobacillus clausii</italic> or <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic>) and <italic toggle="yes">Saccharomyces boulardii</italic> [<xref rid="bib15" ref-type="bibr">15</xref>]. Among them, probiotic <italic toggle="yes">Alkalihalobacillus clausii</italic> (basionym <italic toggle="yes">Bacillus clausii</italic>) has been studied for variety of acute and infectious diarrheal diseases, such as acute and chronic diarrhea, acute community-acquired diarrhea (ACAD), antibiotic associated diarrhea (AAD), <italic toggle="yes">Clostridium difficile</italic>-induced diarrhea (CDID) across different geographical locations. The adjunctive treatment with <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> strains has been reported safe among children, adult and elderly population [<xref rid="bib16" ref-type="bibr">16</xref>]. It is currently available as an over the counter (OTC) medical product and used as a complementary treatment [<xref rid="bib17" ref-type="bibr">17</xref>].</p><p id="p0030"><italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> (average genome size 4197324–4598557 bp and 42.8–44.75% GC content), a sporogenous probiotic bacteria belongs to genus <italic toggle="yes">Alkalihalobacillus</italic> and is widely studied for the production of high alkaline proteases, antimicrobials like type-A lantibiotic clausin (M<sub>w</sub> 2107.94–5,158.11 Da) and other lantibiotics [<xref rid="bib18" ref-type="bibr">18</xref>, <xref rid="bib19" ref-type="bibr">19</xref>]. <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> maintains gut health by improving digestive microenvironment, reprogramming intestinal microbiota and regulating host's immunity [<xref rid="bib20" ref-type="bibr">20</xref>, <xref rid="bib21" ref-type="bibr">21</xref>, <xref rid="bib22" ref-type="bibr">22</xref>]. The naturally encapsulated coating of bacterial spores provides protection against various drought conditions such as high temperature, desiccation, osmotic pressure, etc. This highly resilient allochthonous probiotic can survive and proliferate in harsh gastrointestinal conditions comprising gastric acid, pepsin, pancreatin, ions, digestive enzymes, biles and mucins [<xref rid="bib23" ref-type="bibr">23</xref>]. The efficacy of probiotic <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> varies among strains; differs as per dosages used in the finished formulations and severity of clinical conditions in order to exhibit the intended health benefits [<xref rid="bib12" ref-type="bibr">12</xref>, <xref rid="bib20" ref-type="bibr">20</xref>, <xref rid="bib24" ref-type="bibr">24</xref>].</p><p id="p0035"><italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> strains have long been consumed safely by the general human population [<xref rid="bib24" ref-type="bibr">24</xref>]. <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> is considered as the Qualified Presumption of Safety (QPS) listed bacteria by the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) [<xref rid="bib25" ref-type="bibr">25</xref>]. <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> strains show resistance to one or multiple antibiotics; however, the relevant genes are intrinsically present in chromosomal DNA rendering them highly stable, nontransferable and nonfunctional [<xref rid="bib26" ref-type="bibr">26</xref>, <xref rid="bib27" ref-type="bibr">27</xref>]. In addition, the absence of extrachromosomal genome makes <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> a risk-free and safe probiotic for human and animal applications [<xref rid="bib28" ref-type="bibr">28</xref>]. The intrinsic antibiotic(s) resistance in probiotics can be advantageous as these probiotics can be used in combination with antibiotics to restore microbiota in various gastrointestinal ailments including antibiotic-associated diarrhea [<xref rid="bib24" ref-type="bibr">24</xref>, <xref rid="bib29" ref-type="bibr">29</xref>].</p><p id="p0040">The comparative evaluation on <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> strains showed heterogeneity and variable clinical benefit in different diarrheal conditions. Such effects happen primarily due to differential ability of the strain to survive and germinate under harsh gastrointestinal conditions, the adhesion and colonization on epithelial cells, the modulation immune system, varying compatibility to complex treatment conditions and host adaptability [<xref rid="bib30" ref-type="bibr">30</xref>]. <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> strain with fulfillment of these attributes can provide a consistent therapeutic outcome in gastrointestinal illnesses, thus this study is originated. The current study evaluated the clinical efficacy and safety of the probiotic <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE [MCC 0538] in improving antibiotic-associated diarrhea and related symptoms in pediatric, adolescent and adult population. <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE (genome size 4598557 bp, GC content 44.74%, NCBI Reference Sequence No. <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="pmc:entrez-nucleotide" xlink:href="CP031128">CP031128</ext-link> &amp; <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="pmc:entrez-nucleotide" xlink:href="MH532550">MH532550</ext-link>), a genomically stable and phenotypically safe probiotic bacterium is used in this clinical trial. The frequency of diarrhea, severity of related symptoms and stool consistency in the intervened group and control group were assessed as outcome variables.</p></sec><sec id="sec2"><label>2</label><title>Methods</title><sec id="sec2.1"><label>2.1</label><title>Investigational product (IP) and method of analysis</title><p id="p0045">The investigational product (IP), spore preparation of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE (2 billion colony-forming unit per gram, CFU/g) with excipient (maltodextrin) was used in powder form (one g per sachet). The placebo contained only excipient, maltodextrin (1.00 g). Both test and placebo products were supplied by Advanced Enzyme Technologies Ltd., Thane, India and complied with the standard specifications (Method of Analysis; Supplement File__088AE-AAD_2021). Physical appearance and sensory profile, packaging and labelling were same and only the coded batch numbers could differentiate two products.</p></sec><sec id="sec2.2"><label>2.2</label><title>Ethics and informed consent</title><p id="p0050">The trial was prospectively registered in the Clinical Trial Registry, India [CTRI/2020/03/023936 (13/03/2020)] before patient enrollment began. The written ethical approval obtained from Rajalakshmi Hospital, Karnataka (India) and Sai hospital, Maharashtra (India). Approved study protocol was in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki [<xref rid="bib31" ref-type="bibr">31</xref>], the ICH-harmonized tripartite guideline for good clinical practice [<xref rid="bib32" ref-type="bibr">32</xref>] and the Indian Council of Medical Research Guidelines for Biomedical Research on Human subjects [<xref rid="bib33" ref-type="bibr">33</xref>]; and the same was followed with no further changes or amendments during trial [WHO Format Research Protocol_088AE-AAD(v01) and CONSORT(2010)_Checklist__088AE-AAD_2021]. Written and oral information was provided to all patients in understandable language. Every subject had given written informed consent to investigator after understating the objective of this trial, including possible risks and benefits.</p></sec><sec id="sec2.3"><label>2.3</label><title>Trial design and selection of subjects</title><p id="p0055">The prospective interventional trial was randomized, double-blinded, parallel, placebo controlled and had a total of 5 scheduled visits to the clinical site by the study subjects. Subject selection was based on the defined inclusion and exclusion criteria.</p><sec id="sec2.3.1"><label>2.3.1</label><title>Inclusion criteria</title><p id="p0060">Male and female subjects (2–65 years) were included on following criteria such as – acute infectious diarrhea (three or more loose stools in last 24 h) and treated with physician's prescribed broad spectrum antibiotics (e.g., β-lactam, lincomycin, cephalosporin and macrolide class) for last five days; a positive stool microbial culture test and clinical evaluation by the principal investigator; and willing to participate with written informed consent/assent following applicable guideline.</p></sec><sec id="sec2.3.2"><label>2.3.2</label><title>Exclusion criteria</title><p id="p0065">Patients excluded from study - with bloody or purulent stool, with pus or mucus and severe dehydration needing hospitalization. Subjects with symptoms of septicemia, faster heart rate and breathing, shortness of breath, sweaty or clammy skin were excluded. Subjects were excluded if they were on other bacteriotherapy prior to this study or during study other than interventional product. Subjects with history of gastric and duodenal ulcer, upper gastrointestinal bleeding, autoimmune gastritis and gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) were excluded (Details of Exclusion Criteria; Supplement File__088AE-AAD_2021). In addition, subjects having adverse effects or serious adverse effects, pregnancies, disease emergencies and study protocol violation are removed from the trial (Details of Withdrawal Criteria; Supplement File__088AE-AAD_2021).</p></sec></sec><sec id="sec2.4"><label>2.4</label><title>Randomization and treatment procedures</title><p id="p0070">A total of 120 subjects comprising sixty paediatric subjects (PS, 2–10 years) and sixty from adolescent and adults (AA, 11–65 years) were enrolled. Each age group was allocated with 30 randomized subjects in each of the test and the placebo group. Both the test groups, i.e., paediatric (Test-PS, n = 30) and adolescent and adults (Test-AA, n = 30) were on <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE with two billion colony forming unit activity (Method of Analysis; Supplement File__088AE-AAD_2021) powder (carrier maltodextrin) respectively for twice (bid) and thrice (tid) a day. A similar dosing schedule (on maltodextrin) were given to the respective control [Placebo-PS (n = 30) and Placebo-AA (n = 30)] groups. All subjects were on the prescribed concomitant (ongoing antibiotic therapy) therapy along with IP treatment during the treatment duration. Total study and treatment duration were 17 and 7 days, respectively. The subject randomization (followed by SAS random number generation method), treatment allocation and procedures are represented in a schematic diagram (<xref rid="fig1" ref-type="fig">Figure 1</xref>). Study investigators remained blind until the completion of the study whereas un-blinding was done only at the end of clinical phase completion. Supportive treatments were recommended to the subjects along with IP, if required, but without changing concomitant (antibiotics) treatment as deemed necessary by the investigator. No changes or amendments were made to the approved protocol after the trial commenced and no interim data analysis was done during the study period.<fig id="fig1" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Figure 1</label><caption><p>Schematic diagram of the clinical study on evaluation of the efficacy and safety of <italic toggle="yes">Alkalihalobacillus clausii</italic> 088AE in the treatment of antibiotic-associated diarrhea. The study enrolled total 120 <italic toggle="yes">intension to treat</italic> (ITT) subjects (each 60 subjects in pediatric group and adolescent and adult group) through the inclusion and exclusion criteria screening. Each age group was allocated with 60 subjects (each 30 subjects in test and placebo arm) following the SAS random number generation method. With no adverse effects (AEs) or serious adverse events (SAEs) report and no discontinuation of subjects, completed 120 <italic toggle="yes">per protocol</italic> (PP) subjects were considered for endpoints evaluation. Data comparison between test and placebo, and statistical analysis were performed within age group. Study compliance was checked at every follow up visits by a team of physician-investigator and officers.</p></caption><alt-text id="alttext0025">Figure 1</alt-text><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="gr1.jpg"/></fig></p></sec><sec id="sec2.5"><label>2.5</label><title>Endpoints analysis: efficacy and safety variables</title><p id="p0075">Primary and secondary endpoints evaluated different efficacy and safety variables of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE used for treating antibiotic-associated diarrhea (AAD). This study was conducted on two population groups, i.e., pediatric group and adolescent adult group. Different endpoint results of test arm were compared with the respective placebo arm within specific population group. In primary endpoints, the efficacy of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE was evaluated from time to last unformed stool (TTLUS), total number of unformed stools, time to complete resolution of functional gastrointestinal discomforts and percentage (%) of responders with complete remission of diarrhea at different treatment durations (24–168 h).</p><p id="p0080">Secondary endpoints evaluated changes of severity of AAD related symptoms, visual analog scale (VAS) and tolerance to investigational product at baseline to EOT. Severity of AAD was assessed by physician's investigation for bloating, distension, flatulence, odorous flatulence, difficult gas evacuation, stomach rumbling, belching, bad breath, abdominal movement and excessive gas evacuation. The mean severity score was calculated from a four-point scale on symptoms (0 = none, 1 = mild, 2 = moderate and 3 = Severe). AAD-associated symptoms like abdominal pain, bloating and flatulence, vomiting and nausea, perception of mental wellbeing and influence on daily life were assessed through visual analogue scale (VAS, 0–10). Safety of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE was assessed by examining general physical health, systemic biomarkers and adverse effect reports. The clinical safety was assessed through systemic biomarkers like hematological (complete blood count), hepatic [aspartate aminotransferase (SGOT) and alanine aminotransferase (SGPT)], renal function test (serum concentration of creatinine, albumin, sodium, potassium and blood urea nitrogen), random blood sugar (RBS) and total cholesterol at baseline and EOT. Biomarkers analysis were performed following the standard medical test protocols. The adverse effect (AE) is defined as any medically untoward event detected in a clinical study subject after use of the study agents, whether or not caused by the use of the agents. Whereas, serious adverse event (SAE) is defined as any untoward medical incidence which is life-threatening and results into death or hospitalization, disability or incapacity and congenital anomaly.</p></sec><sec id="sec2.6"><label>2.6</label><title>Sample power and statistical analysis</title><p id="p0085">Following the maximum sample size among primary endpoints, each group with sixty subjects conferred 90% sample power (α = 0.050 when MD = 1.00). Randomization was done using SAS® software, version 9.1.3. Safety and efficacy analysis was performed on per-protocol (PP) population within group. Separate analyses were performed for primary and secondary endpoints. The entire statistical analysis was performed as per the statistical analysis plan (SAP). Significance of treatment effects were determined either by the null-hypothesis (<italic toggle="yes">H</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">0</italic></sub>
<italic toggle="yes">= μ</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">s</italic></sub><italic toggle="yes">-μ</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">e</italic></sub>
<italic toggle="yes">≥ d</italic>) or the alternative hypothesis (<italic toggle="yes">H</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">1</italic></sub>
<italic toggle="yes">= μ</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">s</italic></sub>
<italic toggle="yes">− μ</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">e</italic></sub>
<italic toggle="yes">≤ d</italic>). Where, <italic toggle="yes">μ</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">e</italic></sub> is the mean change in the test arm and <italic toggle="yes">μ</italic><sub><italic toggle="yes">s</italic></sub> is mean change in the placebo arm. Results were analyzed with 5% significance level (confidence interval 95%) and the differences within the groups were assessed using t-test. Differences between two groups were measured using Kruskal-Wallis one-way ANOVA test.</p></sec></sec><sec id="sec3"><label>3</label><title>Results</title><p id="p0090">From March 2020 to October 2020, a total of 60 pediatric and 60 adolescent and adult patients with antibiotic-associated diarrhea (AAD) were enrolled with no exclusion to the study in two hospitals in India. All <italic toggle="yes">intention to treat</italic> (ITT) patients completed the study without dropout, hence, <italic toggle="yes">per protocol’</italic> (PP) population. Pediatric (PS) group enrolled patients within age range of 2–10 years, whereas, adolescent and adults (AA) group enrolled patients within 10–65 years of age. Each age group had two arms with 30 patients per arm and received two different treatments. The test arm of pediatric (Test-PS) and adolescent and adult (Test-AA) groups received <italic toggle="yes">Alkalihalobacillus clausii</italic> 088AE (2 billion per sachet) respectively two and three times in a day. The control arms [pediatric (Placebo-PS) and adolescent and adult (Placebo-AA)] of both groups received maltodextrin with corresponding dosing schedule. Out of 60 patients in pediatric group, Test-PS had total 12 male (M, 40.00%) and 18 females (F, 60.00%) and Placebo-PS had 8M (26.67%):22F (73.33%). In adolescent and adult group, Test-AA had 23M (76.67%) and 7F (23.33%), and Placebo-AA had 22M (73.33%) and 8F (26.67%). Demographic parameters (age, height, body weight and body mass index) of all treatment arms compared within age group were not significantly different (<xref rid="tbl1" ref-type="table">Table 1</xref>). Principal investigator and clinical trial team assessed study regulations at each visit along with all the safety and efficacy assays as per the schedule of events (<xref rid="tbl2" ref-type="table">Table 2</xref>). Subjects reported an acute or persistent mild to severe form of antibiotic-associated diarrhea mainly due β-lactam, lincomycin, cephalosporin and macrolide class antibiotics before enrollment began. Enrolled patients were treated with <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE along with ongoing concomitant antibiotics. IP treatment was started on visit 1 (baseline, day 1) and <italic toggle="yes">end of treatment</italic> was on visit 5 (EOT, day 8). All patients completed the study, reported no drop out, and missed dosage or discontinuation of investigational product. The safety and efficacy analyses were evaluated on PP population, i.e., <italic toggle="yes">full analysis set</italic> (FAS, n = 60) within the age group. The clinical trial was concluded after the telephonic follow up [on visit 06 (day 17 ± 3)] of the last enrolled patient and completion of target sample size according to the study protocol.<table-wrap position="float" id="tbl1" orientation="portrait"><label>Table 1</label><caption><p>The demographic details of pediatric (PS) and adolescent and adult (AA) subjects of four treatment arms (Test-PS and colspan="1" rowspan="1"/><td colspan="1" rowspan="1"/></tr><tr><td colspan="1" rowspan="1">Primary endpoints</td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1"/><td colspan="1" rowspan="1"><italic rowspan="1"><italic toggle="yes">√</italic></td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1"/><td colspan="1" rowspan="1"/></tr><tr><td colspan="1" rowspan="1">Concomitant medications</td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1"/><td colspan="1" rowspan="1"><italic toggle="yes">√</italic></td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1"><italic toggle="yes">√</italic></td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1"><italic toggle="yes">√</italic></td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1"><italic toggle="yes">√</italic></td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1">√</td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1">√</td></tr><tr><td colspan="1" rowspan="1">AE/SAE assessment</td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1"/><td colspan="1" rowspan="1"><italic toggle="yes">√</italic></td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1"><italic toggle="yes">√</italic></td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1"><italic toggle="yes">√</italic></td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1"><italic toggle="yes">√</italic></td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1">√</td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1">√</td></tr></tbody></table><table-wrap-foot><fn id="tbl2fna"><label>a</label><p id="ntpara0010">Visit 01 was for screening, randomization and initiation of treatment (baseline).</p></fn></table-wrap-foot><table-wrap-foot><fn id="tbl2fnb"><label>b</label><p id="ntpara0015">Visit 02 was second day of treatment.</p></fn></table-wrap-foot><table-wrap-foot><fn id="tbl2fnc"><label>c</label><p id="ntpara0020">Visit 03 was third day of treatment.</p></fn></table-wrap-foot><table-wrap-foot><fn id="tbl2fnd"><label>d</label><p id="ntpara0025">Visit 04 was fifth day of treatment.</p></fn></table-wrap-foot><table-wrap-foot><fn id="tbl2fne"><label>e</label><p id="ntpara0030">Visit 05 was eighth day of treatment, i.e., end of treatment (EOT).</p></fn></table-wrap-foot><table-wrap-foot><fn id="tbl2fnf"><label>f</label><p id="ntpara0035">Visit 06 was on 17 ± 3 day and for telephonic follow up.</p></fn></table-wrap-foot><table-wrap-foot><fn id="tbl2fng"><label>g</label><p id="ntpara0040">Visit 07 was unscheduled visit.</p></fn></table-wrap-foot></table-wrap></p><sec id="sec3.1"><label>3.1</label><title>Primary endpoint: efficacy evaluation</title><sec id="sec3.1.1"><label>3.1.1</label><title>Total number of unformed stools</title><p id="p0095">Treatment of AAD with <italic toggle="yes">Alkalihalobacillus clausii</italic> 088AE decreased the total number of unformed stools in pediatrics as well as in adolescent and adult groups. In pediatric group, treatment of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE reduced 16.91% of total number of unformed stools by 24 h compared to placebo where no reduction was recorded from the baseline (average total 103.5 diarrheal episodes at baseline for both arms). Importantly, <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE (Test-PS) improved diarrheal condition in pediatric group by 99.03% at the end of treatment (EOT, 168 h), whereas, 28.50% in placebo (Placebo-PS) arm (p &lt; 0.0001) (<xref rid="fig2" ref-type="fig">Figure 2</xref>). A 57.74% drop in total number of unformed stools was recorded after 24 h of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE treatment in adolescent and adult groups compared to placebo (11.03%). After 96 h of treatment, <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE (Test-AA) arm reported a few (1.41%) incidence of unformed stools compared to placebo (Placebo-AA, 71.72%) (<xref rid="fig2" ref-type="fig">Figure 2</xref>).<fig id="fig2" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Figure 2</label><caption><p>Total number of unformed stools (induced by antibiotic-associated diarrhea) recorded in pediatric# (Placebo-PS and Test-PS) and adolescent and adult∗ (Placebo-AA and Test-AA) groups from the baseline and first day of <italic toggle="yes">Alkalihalobacillus clausii</italic> 088AE administration to the end of treatment (EOT) (<sup>#/</sup>∗p &lt; 0.0001).</p></caption><alt-text id="alttext0030">Figure 2</alt-text><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="gr2.jpg"/></fig></p></sec><sec id="sec3.1.2"><label>3.1.2</label><title>Time to last unformed stool (TTLUS)</title><p id="p0100">Efficacy of <italic toggle="yes">Alkalihalobacillus clausii</italic> 088AE in improving antibiotic-associated diarrhea was determined from frequency of subjects reporting time to last unformed stools following Bristol stool form scale. Incidence of ‘normal’ Bristol stool (type 3 or 4) for the first time was captured by subjects frequency to express TTLUS. In pediatric group, <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE improved the diarrheal conditions by reporting higher frequency normal stools [n2 at 72 h (6.67%), n16 at 96 h (53.33%) and n12 at 168 h (40.00%)] within shorter duration compared to placebo group [n1 at 96 h (3.33%). Similarly, diarrheal condition was improved by <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE in adolescent and adult groups by higher TTLUS [n4 at 48 (26.67%), n17 at 72 h (56.67%) and n1 at 96 h (3.33%)] compared to placebo group [n3 at 48 h (10%) and n7 at 72 h (23.33%)] (<xref rid="fig3" ref-type="fig">Figure 3</xref>).<fig id="fig3" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Figure 3</label><caption><p>The complete remission of diarrhea and relative percentage (%) of responders on time to last unformed stool (TTLUS) at different time points from both pediatric (Placebo-PS and Test-PS) and adolescent and adult (Placebo-AA and Test-AA) groups after the administration of <italic toggle="yes">Alkalihalobacillus</italic> clausii 088AE to the end of treatment (EOT).</p></caption><alt-text id="alttext0035">Figure 3</alt-text><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="gr3.jpg"/></fig></p></sec><sec id="sec3.1.3"><label>3.1.3</label><title>Complete remission of diarrhea [by Bristol stool scale]</title><p id="p0105">Based on Bristol Stool Form Scale (BSFC) questionnaire, percentage responders as defined by the number of patients who reported the ‘normal’ stool form [type 3 (like a sausage but with cracks on its surface) or type 4 (like a sausage or snake, smooth and soft] at different visits were considered to calculate the complete remission of diarrhea. The <italic toggle="yes">Alkalihalobacillus clausii</italic> 088AE-mediated improvement was reflected by percentage responders with complete remission of diarrhea at different visits both in pediatric and adult and adolescents compared placebo. In pediatric group, normal stool appearance was reported by 30 patients at different time points (16 patients in 96 h, 2 patients in 72 h and 12 patients in 168 h) in <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE treatment arm (Test-PS) compared to Placebo-PS (1 patient in 48 h) [p &lt; 0.0001; RR = 0.03 (95%CI, 0.01–0.23); ARR = 0.97 (95%CI, 0.79–0.99)]. In adolescent and adult group, total 22 patients (04 patients in 48 h, 17 patients in 72 h and 1 patient in 96 h) reported complete remission of diarrhea from <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE treatment arm (Test-AA), whereas, 10 patients reported from Placebo-AA arm (3 patients in 48 h and 7 patients in 72 h) [p &lt; 0.0001; RR = 2.20 (95%CI, 1.27–3.81); ARR = -0.40 (95%CI, -0.58–0.15); OR = 5.50 (95%CI, 1.81–16.68)] (<xref rid="fig4" ref-type="fig">Figure 4</xref>).<fig id="fig4" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Figure 4</label><caption><p>Total frequency of complete remission from antibiotic-associated diarrhea (AAD) treated with <italic toggle="yes">Alkalihalobacillus clausii</italic> 088AE compared to respective placebo arms in two treatment groups, i.e., pediatric, adolescent and adult groups.</p></caption><alt-text id="alttext0040">Figure 4</alt-text><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="gr4.jpg"/></fig></p></sec></sec><sec id="sec3.2"><label>3.2</label><title>Secondary endpoints: safety evaluation</title><sec id="sec3.2.1"><label>3.2.1</label><title>Change in severity of AAD related symptoms</title><p id="p0110">Severity of AAD was determined on a four-point scale for symptoms like bloating, distension, flatulence, odorous flatulence, difficult gas evacuation, stomach rumbling, belching, bad breath, abdominal movement and excessive gas evacuation. In current study, treatment with <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE (test arms) significantly reduced the severity score of AAD in pediatric, adolescent and adult groups compared to respective placebo arms. At baseline, severity scores were not significantly different between test and placebo arm in pediatric group [p = 0.1231 (95%CI, -0.05–0.45)] and adolescent and adult group [p = 0.9554 (95%CI, -0.15–0.14)]. In pediatric group, <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE reduced the severity of AAD gradually on each visit, eventually 12.39 folds reduction on EOT compared to placebo arm [mean difference (MD) = 1.36; p &lt; 0.0001 (95%CI, 1.20–1.52)]. The placebo arm did not show any improvement in AAD severity (<xref rid="fig5" ref-type="fig">Figure 5</xref>). In adolescent and adult group, <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE reduced AAD severity over time and 2.34 folds on EOT than its baseline, and was significantly different compared to placebo arm [MD = 0.20; p = 0.0237 (95%CI, 0.03–0.37)] (<xref rid="fig5" ref-type="fig">Figure 5</xref>).<fig id="fig5" position="float" orientation="portrait"><label>Figure 5</label><caption><p>Changes in investigators assessed severity score of AAD related symptoms at different time points both in pediatric [Placebo-PS (♦) and Test-PS (◊)] and adolescent and adult [Placebo-AA (■;) and Test-AA (□)] groups.</p></caption><alt-text id="alttext0045">Figure 5</alt-text><graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" position="float" orientation="portrait" xlink:href="gr5.jpg"/></fig></p></sec><sec id="sec3.2.2"><label>3.2.2</label><title>VAS assessment of AAD symptoms</title><p id="p0115"><italic toggle="yes">Alkalihalobacillus clausii</italic> 088AE treatment reduced other associated symptoms like abdominal pain, bloating and flatulence, vomiting and nausea in both pediatric, adult and adolescent groups compared to placebo (p &lt; 0.0001). These were assessed through visual analogue scale (VAS, 0–10) assessment. Trial data showed that pediatric subjects from Test-PS arm (<italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE) were relived from abdominal pain [MD -6.67 ± 0.19; 95%CI, -7.06-6.28] than Placebo-PS [MD -0.60 ± 0.26; 95%CI, -1.12–0.09]. In adolescent and adult group, Test-AA arm reported reduced abdominal pain [MD -3.40 ± 0.31; 95%CI,-4.02-2.77] compared to Placebo-AA [MD -2.20 ± 0.26; 95%CI, -2.73–1.67] (<xref rid="tbl3" ref-type="table">Table 3</xref>). The bowel movement (diarrhea) was improved remarkably both in pediatric, adolescent and adult group (p &lt; 0.0001). In pediatric group, the mean VAS score difference for bowel movement (diarrhea) was -6.20 ± 0.23 (95%CI, -6.66–5.73) in <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE treated (Test-PS) arm compared to an insignificant mean difference in Placebo-PS [MD -0.60 ± 0.29; 95%CI, -1.18–0.01]. The adolescent and adult group reported a reduced bowel movement (diarrhea) after <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE treatment [Test-AA, MD 5.04 ± 0.49 (95%CI, -6.02-4.05)] than its Placebo-AA arm [MD -3.56 ± 0.43; 95%CI, -4.43–2.68] (<xref rid="tbl3" ref-type="table">Table 3</xref>).<table-wrap position="float" id="tbl3" orientation="portrait"><label>Table 3</label><caption><p>Comparative visual analogue scale (VAS) scores evaluated in antibiotic-associated diarrhea (AAD) at baseline and EOT in pediatric (Test-PS and Placebo-PS) and adolescent and adult group (Test-AA and Placebo-AA) (±SD). In both groups, test arms received <italic toggle="yes">Alkalihalobacillus clausii</italic> 088AE. Symptoms considered were abdominal pain, diarrhea, bloating and flatulence, nausea and vomiting, perception of mental well-being and influence daily life. Intragroup [MD = baseline-EOT] and intergroup mean differences [in pediatric (MD = Placebo-PS – Test-PS) and adolescent and adult group (MD = Placebo-AA – Test-AA)] for all the symptoms was analyzed through ANOVA and 95% confidence interval (CI) estimation at EOT and mean.</p></caption><alt-text id="alttext0060">Table 3</alt-text><table frame="hsides" rules="groups"><thead><tr><th colspan="1" (Placebo-PS – Test-PS)</td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1"/><td colspan="1" rowspan="1"/><td colspan="1" rowspan="1">-5.20 ± 0.06</td><td colspan="1" rowspan="1">-5.32,-4.33 (at EOT) -5.32,-5.07 (at mean)</td></tr></tbody></table></table-wrap></p><p id="p0120">Similarly, pediatric group showed a remarkable improvement in bloating and flatulence symptoms after <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE treatment [Test-PS, MD -6.10 ± 0.16 (95%CI, -6.42–5.77)] compared to Placebo-PS arm [MD 0.60 ± 0.25; 95%CI, -1.10–0.09] (p &lt; 0.0001). The mean difference between Test-AA and Placebo-AA arm was however small in adolescent and adult group [MD -0.33 ± 0.06; 95%CI, -0.46,-0.19] (p &lt; 0.0001). Simultaneously, Test-PS arm of pediatric group reported a sharp reduction of nausea and vomiting symptoms after <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE treatment [MD -6.27 ± 0.12; 95%CI, -6.51–6.02] than Placebo-PS arm [MD -0.76 ± 0.30; 95%CI, -1.36–0.15] (p &lt; 0.0001). Whereas, adolescent and adult group reported a marginal improvement in nausea and vomiting in Test-AA arm [MD -1.93 ± 0.31; 95%CI, -2.56–1.29] than Placebo-AA [MD -1.40 ± 0.29; 95%CI, -1.99–0.80] (p &lt; 0.0001) (<xref rid="tbl3" ref-type="table">Table 3</xref>).</p><p id="p0125">The perception of mental wellbeing and influence on daily life were improved in subjects receiving <italic toggle="yes">Alkalihalobacillus clausii</italic> 088AE. The perception of mental wellbeing of pediatric group was ‘severe’ to ‘very sever’ in both Test-PS and Placebo-PS at baseline [p = 0.1534 (95%CI, -0.21–1.28)]. However, the mental wellbeing was improved over time after <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE intervention (Test-PS) and significantly normalized at EOT [MD -6.54 ± 0.35; 95%CI, -7.23–5.84] (p &lt; 0.0001). In comparison to Test-PS, mental wellbeing was not improved from baseline to EOT in Placebo-PS [MD -0.73 ± 0.28; 95%CI, -1.29–0.16]. The perception of mental wellbeing was ‘mild’ to ‘moderate’ in adolescent and adult group and it was improved from baseline to EOT in Test-AA arm compared to Placebo-AA arm [MD -0.50 ± 0.06; 95%CI, -0.63–0.36] (<xref rid="tbl3" ref-type="table">Table 3</xref>). Similarly, intervention of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE improved influence on daily life was found improved both in pediatric [Test-PS, MD -5.20 ± 0.06 (95%CI, -5.32–5.07)] and adolescent and adult [Test-AA, MD -1.49 ± 0.12 (95%CI, -1.74–1.23)] group compared to their respective placebo arms (p &lt; 0.0001) (<xref rid="tbl3" ref-type="table">Table 3</xref>).</p></sec><sec id="sec3.2.3"><label>3.2.3</label><title>Assessment of IP tolerance, adverse events (AEs) and serious adverse effects (SAEs) and systematic biomarkers</title><p id="p0130">The investigational product (IP), <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE was tolerated well by the study participants. They reported no adverse events (AEs), serious adverse effects (SAEs) or adverse drug reactions (ADRs) during study period.</p><p id="p0135">All vital signs like pulse, respiratory rate, systolic blood pressure, diastolic blood pressure and body temperature were assessed for adolescent and adult group at each visit (<xref rid="appsec1" ref-type="sec">Table S1</xref>). All vital parameters, except, systolic and diastolic blood pressure were measured in pediatric subjects at each visit (<xref rid="appsec1" ref-type="sec">Table S2</xref>). No significant differences (<italic toggle="yes">p</italic> &lt; 0.05) were observed in vital parameters in Test-AA [<italic toggle="yes">p</italic><sup>min</sup> = 0.075 and <italic toggle="yes">p</italic><sup>max</sup> = 0.916] and Test-PS [<italic toggle="yes">p</italic><sup>min</sup> = 0.143 and <italic toggle="yes">p</italic><sup>max</sup> = 0.917] compared to their respective Placebo arms among all visits and results remained within the normal range.</p><p id="p0140">The complete blood count (hemoglobin, total RBC and leukocyte count, neutrophils, lymphocytes, eosinophils, monocytes, basophils, hematocrit, platelet counts, erythrocyte sedimentation rate) in hematology, liver [serum glutamic-oxaloacetic transaminase (SGOT), serum glutamic pyruvic transaminase (SGPT)] and renal (creatinine, blood urea nitrogen, albumin, serum sodium and potassium level) function test and serum biochemistry (total cholesterol and random blood sugar) produced no statistically significant difference (p &lt; 0.05) between baseline (visit 1) and EOT (visit 5) in adolescent and adult [Test-AA and Placebo-AA; <italic toggle="yes">p</italic><sup>min</sup> = 0.063 (95%CI, -0.987–0.027) and <italic toggle="yes">p</italic><sup>max</sup> = 0.945 (95% CI, -1.411–1.510)] (<xref rid="appsec1" ref-type="sec">Table S3</xref>) and pediatric [Test-PS and Placebo-PS; <italic toggle="yes">p</italic><sup>min</sup> = 0.068 (95% CI, -3.304–0.124) and <italic toggle="yes">p</italic><sup>max</sup> = 1.000 (95% CI, -0.189–0.189)] (<xref rid="appsec1" ref-type="sec">Table S4</xref>) groups. These clinical safety parameter results were within standard range of reference values.</p></sec></sec></sec><sec id="sec4"><label>4</label><title>Discussion</title><p id="p0145">Gut microbial <italic toggle="yes">dysbiosis</italic> is a known cause for many gastrointestinal ailments including antibiotic-associated diarrhea (AAD) [<xref rid="bib34" ref-type="bibr">34</xref>, <xref rid="bib35" ref-type="bibr">35</xref>, <xref rid="bib36" ref-type="bibr">36</xref>]. Probiotics offer therapeutic solution to such disorders within gut microbiota. Probiotic strains of <italic toggle="yes">Alkalihalobacillus clausii</italic> lessen AAD-related clinical symptoms by reprogramming the microbial balance of gut; restore healthy and complex host-microbiota interactions. However, heterogeneous study designs often demonstrated variable probiotic efficacies in various gastrointestinal ailments including AAD. These are majorly due to the variability in host-specific clinical circumstances and strain-specific probiotic attributes.</p><p id="p0150">In this CONSORT-compliant randomized placebo-controlled trial (RCT), <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE is evaluated for its therapeutic effectiveness in antibiotic-associated diarrhea (AAD) and related symptoms in pediatric, adolescent and adult population [CONSORT(2010)_Checklist__088AE-AAD_2021]. <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE, MCC 0538 (genome size 4598557 bp, GC content 44.74%, NCBI Reference Sequence No. <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="pmc:entrez-nucleotide" xlink:href="CP031128">CP031128</ext-link> &amp; <ext-link xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" ext-link-type="pmc:entrez-nucleotide" xlink:href="MH532550">MH532550</ext-link>) is a genomically stable and phenotypically safe probiotic bacterium.</p><p id="p0155">The intervention of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE unveiled significant improvement in total number of unformed stools and time to last unformed stool (TTLUS) in pediatrics (Test-PS) as well as in adolescent and adult (Test-AA) compared to their respective placebo groups (Placebo-PS and Placebo-AA). Children are extremely vulnerable to many diarrheal conditions like, acute, infectious, viral and antibiotic-associated diarrhea [<xref rid="bib16" ref-type="bibr">16</xref>]. In this study, pediatric group (children below 10 years of age) reported a significant reduction of total number of unformed stools by 16.91% after 24 h and 99.03% after 168 h (EOT) of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE (4 billion CFU per day) intervention compared to placebo arm (p &lt; 0.0001) (<xref rid="fig2" ref-type="fig">Figure 2</xref>). Several other reports mentioned about <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic>-intervened decrease in number and frequency of stools in children suffered from acute diarrhea. Maugo [<xref rid="bib37" ref-type="bibr">37</xref>] reported a significant decrease in mean number of diarrhoeal motions on third and fourth day of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> treatment (4 billion CFU per day) in children (&lt;5 y, n = 136) with acute diarrhea with severe dehydration. In another study, a same strength and dosage of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> reduced the frequency and duration of diarrhea in children (&lt;12 y, n = 131) after 24 and 60 h of treatment [<xref rid="bib38" ref-type="bibr">38</xref>]. <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE (Test-PS) reported maximum frequency of cessation of diarrhea and complete recovery to normal stools (100%) within average shorter duration of 5.04 day. The shorter duration of therapeutic effect was observed within 48 h of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE treatment. In contrary, 96.7% pediatric patients reported no cessation of diarrhea from Placebo-PS arm even after EOT (168 h). The mean frequency of loose stools (diarrhea) in Test-PS and Placebo-PS was 3.43 ± 0.07 and 3.47 ± 0.11 at baseline [p = 0.0983 (95%CI, -0.01–0.09)]; which was changed to 0.03 ± 0.01 and 2.47 ± 0.04 at EOT [p &lt; 0.0001 (95%CI, 2.42–2.45)], respectively. These significant results clearly indicated that <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE was effective against AAD by decreasing diarrheal frequency and duration and improving consistency of stools among children. Sudha et al. [<xref rid="bib39" ref-type="bibr">39</xref>] reported about drop of stools frequency and increase in stool consistency among children (&lt;5 y, n = 119) receiving <italic toggle="yes">B. clausii</italic> suspension after 96 h of treatment (4<sup>th</sup> day). In an open-label study reported by De Castro et al. [<xref rid="bib40" ref-type="bibr">40</xref>], <italic toggle="yes">B. clausii</italic> (2–4 billion CFU per day) resolved diarrhea (52.6 %) with reduced stools frequency within first 3 days of treatment in Filipino children (&lt;6 y, n = 3178) suffered with acute community-acquired diarrhea of viral origin or antibiotic administration. However, the IP, compounded with four different strains of <italic toggle="yes">B. clausii</italic>, e.g., O/C, SIN, N/R, and T observed low rate of adverse events among study subjects. Shah et al. [<xref rid="bib41" ref-type="bibr">41</xref>], in an interesting study (n = 225), determined the comparative therapeutic efficacy between <italic toggle="yes">B. clausii</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">L</italic>actic <italic toggle="yes">A</italic>cid <italic toggle="yes">B</italic>acillus (LAB) in children (&lt;5 y). The study showed that a 4 billion CFU/day of <italic toggle="yes">B. clausii</italic> along with ORS + Zinc supplement showed better efficacy than LAB in terms of faster recovery and achieving normal stool frequency. In fact, other spore-forming <italic toggle="yes">Bacillus</italic> like <italic toggle="yes">B. subtilis</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">B. coagulans</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">B. licheniformis</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">Clostridium butyricum</italic> and <italic toggle="yes">Lactobacillus</italic> spp., <italic toggle="yes">Pediococcus</italic> spp., <italic toggle="yes">Saccharomyces boulardii</italic> have clinically evaluated to exert therapeutic efficacies against various pediatric diarrhea including antibiotic-associated diarrhea [<xref rid="bib2" ref-type="bibr">2</xref>, <xref rid="bib13" ref-type="bibr">13</xref>, <xref rid="bib42" ref-type="bibr">42</xref>].</p><p id="p0160">Similar to improvement in diarrheal conditions in children, <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE (6 billion CFU per day) treatment reduced total number of unformed stool in adolescent and adult group by 57.74% after 24 h compared to placebo arm (<italic toggle="yes">p &lt;</italic> 0.0001) (<xref rid="fig2" ref-type="fig">Figure 2</xref>). At baseline, both Placebo-AA and Test-AA had mean diarrheal frequency of 4.83 ± 0.29 and 4.73 ± 0.17 [<italic toggle="yes">p =</italic> 0.1087 (95%CI, -0.22–0.02)]; which was changed to 3.47 ± 0.12 and 0.00 ± 0.00 [<italic toggle="yes">p &lt;</italic> 0.0001 (95%CI, -3.51–3.42)], respectively. Treatment with <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE reported higher time to last unformed stools, viz., 26.67, 56.67 and 3.33% respectively after 48, 72 and 96h (<xref rid="fig3" ref-type="fig">Figure 3</xref>). Results of clinical effectiveness of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE are in agreement with other strains reported [<xref rid="bib43" ref-type="bibr">43</xref>]. Earlier, Sudha et al. [<xref rid="bib43" ref-type="bibr">43</xref>] reported on <italic toggle="yes">B. clausii</italic> strain UBBC07 which reduced the mean duration and frequency of acute diarrhoea, with improvement in stool consistency in a second phase clinical trial (n = 27). In another study, Plomer et al. [<xref rid="bib44" ref-type="bibr">44</xref>] reported about therapeutic effectiveness of a commercially available medicinal product Enterogermina®, contains four different strains of poly-antibiotic resistant <italic toggle="yes">B. clausii</italic> (O/C, SIN, N/R and T) that decreased the incidence (39%) and duration of diarrhea in patients (n = 130) receiving <italic toggle="yes">H. pylori</italic> eradication therapy. Several other pathogens like <italic toggle="yes">C. perfringens</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">S. aureus</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">K. oxytoca</italic>, <italic toggle="yes">Candida</italic> spp., <italic toggle="yes">Pseudomonas</italic> spp. and <italic toggle="yes">Salmonella</italic> spp. infrequently distort the intestinal microbial ecology. β-lactam, lincomycin, cephalosporin and macrolide class of antibiotics are routinely applied to control such pathogenic overgrowth that often induce adverse effects like infectious or antibiotic-associated diarrhea [<xref rid="bib45" ref-type="bibr">45</xref>]. Certainly, the compatibility of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE with antibiotics is a key attribute behind its therapeutic effectiveness against gastrointestinal ailments including antibiotic induced infectious diarrhea.</p><p id="p0165">The antibiotic-associated diarrheal severity is associated with symptoms like bloating, fever, distension, flatulence, odorous flatulence, difficult gas evacuation, stomach rumbling, belching, bad breath, abdominal movement and excessive gas evacuation. In this study, <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE showed significant reduction in severity scores on EOT in pediatric [<italic toggle="yes">p &lt;</italic> 0.0001 (95%CI, -1.52–1.21)] as well as adolescent and adult [<italic toggle="yes">p =</italic> 0.0237 (95%CI, 0.03–0.37)] groups compared to their respective placebo arms. Few other studies also evaluated severity parameters during AAD. With a triple-therapy RCT study [rabeprazole 20 mg-bid, clarithromycin 500 mg-bid, amoxicillin 1 g-bid and <italic toggle="yes">B. clausii</italic> 2 billion CFU-tid (n = 130)] on <italic toggle="yes">H. pylori</italic>-positive patients, Plomer et al. [<xref rid="bib44" ref-type="bibr">44</xref>] reported that <italic toggle="yes">B. clauii</italic> reduced (29%) incidence of diarrhea in first week and remained lower in second week. In secondary efficacy outcomes, <italic toggle="yes">B. clausii</italic> with triple-therapy reduced the patient-reported frequency/intensity of associated symptoms like vomiting, taste disturbance, loss of appetite, nausea, epigastric pain, flatulence, constipation, or skin rash from first to second week. In a similar triple-therapy, Nista et al. [<xref rid="bib46" ref-type="bibr">46</xref>] reported on lower incidence of nausea, diarrhea and epigastric pain in <italic toggle="yes">Helicobacter pylori</italic>-positive patients (n = 120) after 14 days of <italic toggle="yes">B. clausii</italic> treatment. On a similar note, this study evaluated AAD-associated symptoms on patients receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics treatment and recorded the degree of improvement using VAS assessment scale. Results indicated that <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE was efficacious in reducing symptoms like abdominal pain, bloating and flatulence, vomiting and nausea, perception of mental wellbeing and influence on daily life in both pediatric, adult and adolescent groups compared to placebo (p &lt; 0.05). The improvement [change between two arm means (Test <italic toggle="yes">vs.</italic> Placebo) on EOT and mean change between baseline to EOT means of two arms] was time-dependent and measured statistically significant on EOT (p &lt; 0.0001) compared to respective placebo. Interestingly, a comparative analysis implied on <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE that might exert better clinical efficacies than other commercially available poly-antibiotic resistant <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> strains. This can be due to distinguished gastrointestinal stability characteristics, antipathogenic and immunomodulatory profile of the current strain <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE. Urdaci et al. [<xref rid="bib47" ref-type="bibr">47</xref>] particularly demonstrated the inhibitory activity of <italic toggle="yes">B. clausii</italic> OC against <italic toggle="yes">S. aureus</italic> CIP35053156, <italic toggle="yes">E. faecium</italic> LMBA27323 and <italic toggle="yes">Clostridium difficile</italic> 514. <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> supports the restoration of intestinal microbiota, aids in improving digestion and absorption of nutrients, antibiotic-induced vitamin deficiency and may facilitate systematic detoxification of residual antibiotics [<xref rid="bib48" ref-type="bibr">48</xref>, <xref rid="bib49" ref-type="bibr">49</xref>]. Diarrheal severity varies on grade of inflammation of mucosal lining. <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> may modulate various inflammasome markers like nuclear factor κβ (NF-kβ), mitogen-activated protein kinases (MAPK), nitric oxide synthase (NOS), γ-interferon (IFN-γ) and tumor necrosis factor (TNF) [<xref rid="bib47" ref-type="bibr">47</xref>, <xref rid="bib50" ref-type="bibr">50</xref>]. Increasing evidences support that <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> can modulate epithelial barrier and resume gastrointestinal homeostasis with the differential expression of genes related to immune response and inflammation (IL-8, IL-1β and IL-1 receptor ligands, CD79β, FCGR2β, β-defensin, IFN-β), apoptosis and cell growth (caspase 5, BCL2-antagonist), cell differentiation (IL-13), cell-cell signaling (IL6R), cell adhesion (protocadherin 12, vitronectin, type 2-cadherin 6), signal transcription and transduction (MAX dimerization protein 1, NF-κβ binding protein), tight junction proteins (mucin 5AC, occludin and zonula occludens-1) [<xref rid="bib51" ref-type="bibr">51</xref>, <xref rid="bib52" ref-type="bibr">52</xref>, <xref rid="bib53" ref-type="bibr">53</xref>].</p><p id="p0170">Safety risk assessment unveiled that the investigational spore preparation of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE (2 billion CFU) was well tolerated by pediatric (bid) and adolescent and adult (tid) group when administered with antibiotics. <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE was safe in both pediatric (Test-PS and Placebo-PS) and adolescent and adult (Test-AA and Placebo-AA) groups as no statistically significant difference was estimated between baseline (visit 1) and EOT (visit 5) for vital signs, hematology, liver and renal function test and serum biochemistry parameters (p &lt; 0.05). Each safety parameter result was within standard range of reference values. Simultaneously, no study drug related adverse events (AEs), serious adverse effects (SAEs) or adverse drug reactions (ADRs) were noted during the trial, which conclude that investigational product is safe to use. In contrary to the safety of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE, other strains of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> have been reported for adverse effects of mild to moderate severity in a very small group of study participants [<xref rid="bib24" ref-type="bibr">24</xref>, <xref rid="bib44" ref-type="bibr">44</xref>]. In many clinical studies, spore preparation of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> is administered orally with a dosage of 1–4 × 10<sup>9</sup> CFU/day to neonates, infants and children and 2–8×10<sup>9</sup> CFU/day to adults [<xref rid="bib16" ref-type="bibr">16</xref>, <xref rid="bib24" ref-type="bibr">24</xref>, <xref rid="bib38" ref-type="bibr">38</xref>, <xref rid="bib43" ref-type="bibr">43</xref>, <xref rid="bib50" ref-type="bibr">50</xref>, <xref rid="bib53" ref-type="bibr">53</xref>, <xref rid="bib54" ref-type="bibr">54</xref>, <xref rid="bib55" ref-type="bibr">55</xref>].</p><p id="p0175">In summary, 2 × 10<sup>9</sup> CFU of probiotic <italic toggle="yes">Alkalihalobacillus clausii</italic> 088AE (basionym <italic toggle="yes">Bacillus clausii</italic> 088AE) was widely accepted by children (bid) and adolescents and adults (tid) with no treatment-related adverse reactions. Co-administration of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE with antibiotics can significantly reduce diarrhea and alleviate the symptoms of diarrhea induced by antibiotics, such as abdominal pain, diarrhea (defecation), bloating and flatulence, nausea and vomiting, perception of mental well-being and influence daily life, compared to those placebo arms. Treatment with <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE significantly reduced stool frequency and shortened the duration of unformed stools with "normal" stool consistency, reducing the severity of AAD. No serious adverse reactions further confirmed the treatment safety and therapeutic effects of <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE. <italic toggle="yes">A. clausii</italic> 088AE can be used as an effective adjunct bacterial therapy for the pathophysiology of diarrhea, especially AAD and acute infectious diarrhea in children, adolescents, and adults.</p></sec><sec id="sec5"><title>Declarations</title><sec id="sec5.1"><title>Author contribution statement</title><p id="p0180">Chiranjit Maity: Conceived and designed the experiments; Performed the experiments; Analyzed and interpreted the data; Wrote the paper.</p><p id="p0185">Anil Kumar Gupta: Conceived and designed the experiments; Analyzed and interpreted the data.</p></sec><sec id="sec5.2"><title>Funding statement</title><p id="p0190">This work was supported by <funding-source id="gs1">Advanced Enzyme Technologies Ltd.</funding-source>, Thane, India.</p></sec><sec sec-type="data-availability" id="sec5.3"><title>Data availability statement</title><p id="p0195">Data will be made available on request.</p></sec><sec sec-type="COI-statement" id="sec5.4"><title>Declaration of interests statement</title><p id="p0200">The authors declare no conflict of interest.</p></sec><sec id="sec5.5"><title>Additional information</title><p id="p0205">No additional information is available for this paper.</p></sec></sec></body><back><ref-list id="cebib0010"><title>References</title><ref id="bib1"><label>1</label><element-citation publication-type="journal" id="sref1"><person-group person-group-type="author"><name name-style="western"><surname>Bartlett</surname><given-names>J.G.</given-names></name></person-group><article-title>Antibiotic-associated diarrhea</article-title><source>N. Engl. Environ.
